new_statements.quote: En tzotzil existen dos tipos de acentuación prosódica: A. Las palabras se acentúan sobre la primera sílaba de la raíz, sea ésta simple o compuesta. En cadenas de varias sílabas se acentúa otra sílaba más, de manera que nunca aparezcan más de tres sílabas seguidas sin acento. Ejemplos: cha.c'ü.xu.bi.nún.cu.tíc ustedes tienen misericordia de nosotros / li.vï.ni.que.ti.qué los hombres [...] B. La última sílaba de una oración se acentúa con un aumento en el tono de la última sílaba y un desvanecimiento del mismo. [...] Por el hecho de que la acentuación obedece estas reglas, no es necesario indicarla en forma escrita en el idioma.
new_statements.translation: In Tzotzil there are two kinds of prosodic accentuation: A. Words are accented on the first syllable of the root, whether simple or compound. In strings of several syllables one further syllable is accented, so that never more than three syllables in a row appear without accent. Examples: cha.c'ü.xu.bi.nún.cu.tíc 'you (pl.) have mercy on us' / li.vï.ni.que.ti.qué 'the men' [...] B. The last syllable of a sentence is accented with a rise in the pitch of that last syllable and a fading of it. [...] Because accentuation obeys these rules, it is not necessary to mark it in writing in the language.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable of the lexical root, so prefixes (aspect/person markers, articles) are skipped; in long polysyllabic strings an extra stress is added so that no more than three unstressed syllables run together (in the examples the root-initial syllable is marked with a diaeresis, c'ü / vï, and the added stresses with acute accents, nún, tíc / qué). Separately, the final syllable of a sentence carries a pitch rise-and-fall; the final syllable of a preceding subordinate clause or noun phrase gets the rise without the fall. Laughlin 1975:23 (Zinacantán, same 'central' dialect area as Chenalhó by his classification) and Haviland 1981:14 (Zinacantán) state the same two-level system: root-initial word stress plus phrase-final prominence, with isolated words heard as final-stressed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'En cadenas de varias sílabas se acentúa otra sílaba más, de manera que nunca aparezcan más de tres sílabas seguidas sin acento' — an additional stress is inserted so that at most three unstressed syllables occur in sequence (examples cha.c'ü.xu.bi.nún.cu.tíc; li.vï.ni.que.ti.qué). Laughlin and Haviland mention no secondary word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for the word rule. Laughlin 1975:23 (Zinacantán) notes that in isolation forms stress is not final in affective verbs with -luh, first-person-plural-exclusive suffixed forms and reduplicated disyllabic stems. Haviland 1981:14: particles are unaccented unless phrase-final.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (root-initial) versus sentence/phrase level (final syllable, pitch rise); examples are orthographic and accents were added only to guide the compiler; the book states stress is not. The statement is made for 'tzotzil' as a language, in a San Andrés-based dictionary that samples Chenalhó variants; it is not a Chenalhó-specific description.
new_statements.identity_note: tzot1263 is the Glottolog bookkeeping entry for retired ISO 639-3 code tze 'Chenalhó Tzotzil' (Tzotzil Ch'enalo'), merged into tzo = tzot1259 by ISO change request 2008-061; Glottolog 5.1 attaches no descriptive references to it. No Chenalhó-specific stress statement was found. The quoted statement comes from the ILV dictionary of the San Andrés Larráinzar dialect (= tzot1260), which explicitly samples Chenalhó ('Ch'en') as one of four additional variants and whose grammar was proofread by Manuel Arias Pérez of Chenalhó; the accent rule is stated for Tzotzil as a whole. Laughlin 1975 (Zinacantán = tzot1264) places Chenalhó in the same central dialect area as Zinacantán and gives the same root-initial + phrase-final system. Glottolog's only Chenalhó-coded description is Hopkins 1967 on the neighbouring Chalchihuitán variety (not obtained).

new_statements.quote: [p. 11] Fuera del yucateco, uspanteko y mocho’, que han desarrollado tonos léxicos, las lenguas mayas, incluyendo el tseltal y tsotsil en general, no presentan prosodia contrastiva a nivel de palabra: ni acento tónico contrastivo como el del español, ni tonos (Bennett 2016; England & Baird 2017). En Carranza, las palabras se distinguen según el tono de su sílaba inicial, mientras que las sílabas siguientes reciben un tono predecible, con la excepción de ciertos sufijos. [p. 40] En cambio, tsòtsíl lleva un tono alto en la segunda sílaba, reflejando la acentuación final de tsotsil tanto en español como en tsotsil de Chamula; esto muestra que es un préstamo reciente.
new_statements.translation: [p. 11] Apart from Yucatec, Uspanteko and Mocho', which have developed lexical tones, the Mayan languages, including Tseltal and Tsotsil in general, show no contrastive prosody at the word level: neither contrastive stress like that of Spanish, nor tones (Bennett 2016; England & Baird 2017). In Carranza, words are distinguished by the tone of their initial syllable, while the following syllables receive a predictable tone, with the exception of certain suffixes. [p. 40] By contrast, tsòtsíl carries a high tone on the second syllable, reflecting the final stress of tsotsil both in Spanish and in Chamula Tsotsil; this shows that it is a recent loan.

new_statements.relation_note: Two-sided. (a) The general claim (Tsotsil has no contrastive word prosody) is compatible with the existing Hurley & Ruiz Sánchez 1978 statement, whose root-initial rule is fully predictable, so on that point it refines (adds: non-contrastive, no tone). (b) The concrete placement it names, 'la acentuación final de tsotsil.. en tsotsil de Chamula' (final stress), differs from the existing statement's 'first syllable of the root' (San Andrés base with Chenalhó variants). Chamula is in the same central dialect area as Chenalhó (Laughlin 1975), but the remark is about Chamula, not Chenalhó, and the article's own object is Venustiano Carranza (southern, tonal), which is not this variety. Flagged…
new_statements.rule_in_words: For Tsotsil in general (all varieties except Venustiano Carranza) word-level prosody is non-contrastive: no lexically contrastive stress and no tone, i.e. any word stress is predictable. Venustiano Carranza Tsotsil alone is a tone language (H vs L on the initial syllable, later syllables predictable; sentence-final syllable overridden by phrasal prosody). The one concrete placement statement is incidental: the Spanish loan tsòtsíl surfaces in Carranza with H on its second (final) syllable because Tsotsil (Spanish word tsotsil and the Chamula Tsotsil word) has final stress ('acentuación final'). Nothing is said about Chenalhó by name.
new_statements.exceptions: In Carranza: certain suffixes escape the predictable-tone pattern (p. 12); the sentence-final syllable is written without tone because phrasal prosody replaces the underlying tone there (fn. 6, p. 26). The general no-contrastive-prosody claim excludes Yucatec, Uspanteko, Mocho' and Carranza Tsotsil.
new_statements.identity_note: Polian 2024 describes Venustiano Carranza Tsotsil (southern, tonal), with a side remark on Chamula Tsotsil; it never names Chenalhó. Chamula and Chenalhó are both in Laughlin's central dialect area. The existing statement (Hurley & Ruiz Sánchez 1978) is San Andrés-based with Chenalhó variants marked; Glottolog assigns Hopkins 1967 (Chalchihuitán) to this variety but that sketch is JSTOR-only and not opened.

readall_conflicts: Its general statement (Tsotsil apart from Venustiano Carranza has no contrastive word-level prosody, neither stress nor tone) is compatible with the existing Hurley & Ruiz Sánchez 1978 statement, but its one placement remark, that Chamula Tsotsil has final stress ('acentuación final', p. 40), differs from Hurley & Ruiz Sánchez's 'first syllable of the root' rule (San Andrés base, Chenalhó variants included). The same split already exists among the sources held by the project for the neighbouring Zinacantán dialect: Laughlin 1975 p. 23 gives primary stress on the final syllable of words in isolation but on the root vowel in normal speech, and Haviland 1981 p. 14 gives root-initial word stress plus a stronger phrase-final accent. So the disagreement is most likely word-in-isolation (final) versus word-in-phrase (root-initial) descriptions of one non-contrastive system rather than a dialect difference; Polian 2017 (Routledge), which might settle it for Tsotsil as a whole, remains unopened (paywalled, no OA copy).
